FACILITY DESCRIPTION The Permittee owns and operates a municipal wastewater treatment facility (WWTF) and associated wastewater collection and disposal facilities that serve a population of 1,340 residential, commercial, and industrial users in the community of Redway in Humboldt County. There are no industrial users within the service area. The Facility accepts wastewater from two institutional users located outside of the service area: the Eel River Conservation Camp and a YMCA Camp. Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The Facility is located in the Benbow subarea of the South Fork Eel River Hydrologic Area. The Facility is designed to treat an average dry weather flow of 0.186 mgd, and a peak wet weather flow of 0.580 mgd. 2.1.1. The Dogwood lift station pumps raw wastewater into an 8-inch pressure main down Dogwood Lane, under the South Fork Eel River, and cross-country to the Facility, where it enters the plant distribution box upstream of the oxidation ditch. chunks.text: A pilot-scale plexiglas Carrousel oxidation ditch was constructed, in which three semicircular channels were connected to four 1.15-m long straight channels. The ditch was 0.35-m wide and 0.5-m deep with a total working volume of 1.4 m 3 . Air was introduced from four 1-m long microporous aerator pipes located at the base of the second and third channels. The sketch of the reactor can be found in the supplementary information (SI). Experimental activated sludge was seeded from a steady-running SBR process in a municipal WWTP. The COD and NH 4 + -N concentration of synthetic wastewater were controlled at 250 mg L −1 and 50 mg L −1 , and pH was approximately 7.8 without adjustment. The liquor temperature was maintained at 22 ± 2 °C with a heating rod. Before getting into the inlet of the first channel, the influent and returned sludge were firstly pumped into a 50-L bioselector with continuous blending to avoid sludge bulking problem. The variations of HRT and SRT were achieved by altering the daily influent and sludge discharge rate.

chunks.text: Electrochemical treatment systems have been shown to provide effective treatment of latrine wastewater. Greater than 5-log inactivation of bacterial and viral indicator organisms is achieved via production of reactive chlorine species from chloride (15−20 mM) within 1 h at 4 V applied cell potential. 3 A combination of reactive chlorine species and direct oxidation provide reduction of chemical oxygen demand (COD) 4 and transformation of trace organic contaminants within 4 h (3.5− 4.5 V applied cell potential) 5−7 with rates enhanced at elevated chloride concentrations (up to 75 mM). Under similar operating conditions, ammonium removal occurs via breakpoint chlorination, 8 and phosphorus can be precipitated as hydroxyapatite. 9 Unfortunately, strongly oxidizing conditions in the presence of the high concentrations of chloride and organic matter typical of latrine wastewater also result in formation of toxic byproducts. 10 While wastewater disinfection is essential to protecting human health, an ideal electrochemical system should also be designed to minimize toxic byproduct formation. 11 Chloride enhances electrochemical treatment via formation of reactive chlorine species (e.g., hypochlorous acid, chloramines, and chlorine radicals).

chunks.text: Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) represent a diverse array of water treatment technologies that have generated significant research attention and utilization in a range of water and wastewater treatment applications over the years [1] . Many of the potential and demonstrated applications of AOPs are related to the treatment of industrial wastewater effluents, including those generated from hospitals, slaughterhouses, distilleries, textile mills, and chemical processing plants [2] . Depending on the source, industrial effluents can contain a mixture of complex pollutants, including recalcitrant and toxic organic compounds such as aromatics, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, personal care products, and endocrine-disrupting chemicals. AOPs have been identified as an effective means to treat these complex effluents due to their ability to produce powerful oxidizing agents such as hydroxyl radicals ( • OH) insitu [3] . The strength and non-selectivity of • OH as an oxidizing agent enables the complete mineralization of a wide range of organic compounds at first order rates in the magnitude of 10 6 to 10 9 M − 1 s − 1 [4] .

Drying rates ranged between 1 and 40 g/min/m 2 , leading to drying times comprised between 100 and 300 min. The drying kinetics increased as temperature was higher, and pellet diameter and relative humidity were lower. Temperature had the greatest influence on the drying kinetics (in both the constant and falling rate periods), followed by the effect of pellet diameter. The drying kinetics were affected in a moderate way by the relative humidity in the constant rate period and part of the falling rate period. The air velocity had a slight effect of drying kinetics during the constant rate period, but this becomes insignificant during the falling rate period. The effective diffusivities increased from 7.81 Â 10 À8 to 1.97 Â 10 À7 m 2 /s by increasing the temperature from 40 to 80 C, leading to an activation energy of 23 kJ/mol. These values are typical from those found for wastewater sludge. The sludge exhibited a critical moisture content varying between 2.4 and 3.2 g/g db during drying without a clear trend as a function of the operating conditions and suggested that sludge was composed of considerably more bound moisture than unbound.

chunks.text: Presently, there are approximately 21,600 municipal wastewater treatment facilities serving 226.4 million people (USEPA, 2008) in the U.S. A large amount of biosolids including sludge and scum from these facilities are generated and then disposed either in landfills (28%) or in farmlands (45%, Willis et al., 2012) . This biosolid management practice has caused many environmental pollution and economic stress because biosolids landfilling raises disposal fee for the wastewater treatment facilities and releases methane as a strong greenhouse gas in landfills. Current research shows those biosolid wastes contain a good deal of energy. For example, the sludge collected from the primary and secondary treatment processes contains the energy of 8000 Btu per dry pound and scum contains 11,400 Btu per dry pound (Outwater, 1994; McCarty et al., 2011) . By recovering, utilizing, or selling the energy contained in those wastes, wastewater treatment facilities can reduce not only a large amount of waste disposal to landfills, eliminate the operation cost associated with the old practice, but generate extra revenue for better economic and societal benefit.

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .
